extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; readers interested in philosophy/epistemology of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes principles, standards, and evaluative criteria for scientific inquiry and the production/acceptance of scientific laws (role of imagination, classification, testing, reality/sense-impression criteria, value-claims of science).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of science is to ascertain truth in every possible branch of knowledge. There is no sphere of inquiry which lies outside the legitimate field of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science should not be restricted to narrow domains; drawing artificial distinctions between 'scientific' and 'philosophical' fields is described as obscurantism. Evaluate claims or inquiries by whether they aim to ascertain truth through scientific methods rather than by domain exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful classification and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful and accurate classification of facts and observation of their correlation and sequence are primary features of the scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific work must begin with systematic collection, classification and tracing of relationships and sequences among facts (Darwin's 'systematic inquiry' is cited as example). Good classification in the scientist's mind is prerequisite to discovering laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of laws via disciplined creative imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of scientific laws is achieved by the aid of the creative imagination — a single statement or brief formula that summarizes wide ranges of relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is necessary to invent compact formulae expressing many phenomena (examples: Darwin, Newton); however, this imagination must be 'disciplined' — grounded in an appreciation of the whole range of facts and prior classifications before proposing a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-criticism and public touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-criticism and the final touchstone of equal validity for all normally constituted minds are essential features of the scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After imaginative invention, the discoverer must test and criticise the proposed law 'in every conceivable way' until confident it accords with the whole group of phenomena. The work must withstand impartial criticism and be communicable/validatable by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific use of imagination must be disciplined and tested
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination must appreciate the whole range of facts to be resumed in a law, and once a law is reached it must be tested and criticised by its discoverer until certain it is in real agreement with the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indulging imagination that 'solves the universe' without prior acquaintance with classifications of facts; require prolonged periods of self-criticism and testing (Darwin's multi-year hesitation and testing cited as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgment aligned with empirical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic judgment pronounces for or against an interpretation according as that interpretation embodies or contradicts the phenomena of life; it is only satisfied when the artist's (or scientist's) formula contradicts none of the phenomena it intends to resume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific account is presented as the only interpretation that can permanently satisfy the aesthetic judgment because it will not be entirely contradicted by observation and experience. Evaluate explanatory elegance only insofar as it accords with observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer partial correct solutions over complete wrong solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to be content with the fraction of a right solution than to beguile ourselves with the whole of a wrong solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theories or proposals, prioritize partial but truthful/empirically-grounded results over comprehensive but demonstrably false frameworks — science advances 'line upon line' by incremental, testable improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to public support based on science's social and personal goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of science to our support depend on: (a) the efficient mental training it provides for the citizen; (b) the light it brings to bear on many important social problems; (c) the increased comfort it adds to practical life; (d) the permanent gratification it yields to the aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the societal value of scientific work, consider its contributions to education/citizenship, policy/social problem-solving, practical benefits, and enduring aesthetic/intellectual satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of reality: dependence on sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The reality of a thing depends upon the possibility of its occurring in whole or part as a group of immediate sense-impressions; some immediate sense-impression there must be if we are to term the object real and not merely the product of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about external objects should be assessed by whether they are tied to possible immediate sense-impressions (direct or indirect). This provides a working standard for distinguishing 'real' from 'unreal' in scientific discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: External objects are constructs of immediate and stored sense-impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: An external object is in general a construct—a combination of immediate sense-impressions with past (stored) sense-impressions (memory and associative inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perception involves inference and memory: much of what we call an 'object' is contributed by our past experiences. Evaluations of observational claims should account for constructive aspects of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness and thought depend on stored impressions and brain 'plasticity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness is largely due to the stock of stored impresses and to the manner in which these condition messages to motor nerves; the measure of consciousness depends on (i) extent and variety of past sense-impressions, and (ii) the degree to which the brain can permanently preserve the impress of these sense-impressions (complexity and plasticity of the brain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering cognitive or behavioral claims, evaluate the role of prior experience and memory capacity as determinants of consciousness, thought, and voluntary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary action criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When an exertion follows immediately on a sense-impression it is involuntary (instinct/habit); when conditioned by stored sense-impressions it is voluntary — apparently 'determined from within ourselves' (freedom of will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions by whether they are direct reflexive responses to immediate impressions or are mediated by recalled experiences and deliberation; this distinction bears on attributions of will, responsibility, and intentionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain-as-exchange analogy for evaluating thought processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The brain may be compared to a central telephone exchange: sense-impressions are messages from senders; stored information is the office directory; the 'clerk' links inputs to outputs. Thought and consciousness arise from receipt of messages and the information stored in the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the exchange analogy to analyze mental processes: appreciate that without sense-impressions and memory (stored impresses) there would be no thought; originality is limited to linking inputs to stored information. This guides evaluation of cognitive claims and models.
